title: August Inflation Holds at 3.4% as Fed Rate-Hike Odds Jump to 90%
excerpt: Consumer prices rose 0.4% in August with gasoline up 3.9%, and core inflation stayed firm — putting a September Fed rate hike firmly on the table.
body:
• The consumer price index rose 0.4% in August from July and 3.4% from a year earlier — unchanged from July's annual pace — the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday.
  • Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, rose 0.3% for the month and 2.4% year over year, firmer than expected as price pressures spread beyond fuel.
  • Gasoline prices jumped 3.9% and accounted for a third of the monthly increase, with tech goods and services adding fresh upward pressure.
  • Traders raised the odds of a Federal Reserve rate hike at the September 15-16 meeting to 90% from 70%, according to CME FedWatch.

Price pressures broaden beyond the pump

Inflation held stubbornly high in August, strengthening the case for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates next week. Consumer prices rose 0.4% for the month, an acceleration from July's 0.1% pace, and 3.4% over the past year — the same annual rate as July, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics report released Friday.

Gasoline prices surged 3.9% and accounted for a third of the monthly gain. Underlying inflation also showed signs of spreading: core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy costs, rose 0.3% in August after a 0.2% July increase, and 2.4% over 12 months, down only slightly from 2.5% in July.

After the report, traders boosted the odds of a quarter-point rate hike at the Fed's September 15-16 meeting to 90% from 70% the day before, according to CME FedWatch. The benchmark federal funds rate currently sits in a 3.50%-3.75% range.

Context & Background

Inflation has accelerated since the U.S.-led war with Iran began, driven first by energy. Prices peaked at a 4.2% annual rate in May before cooling through June and July, and economists had hoped August would extend the moderation. Instead, gasoline averaged $4.192 a gallon in August, up from $4.064 in July, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, while Brent crude climbed above $100 as tensions around the Strait of Hormuz persisted.

The August report was the last major inflation reading before the Fed's September meeting. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said last month that the central bank will "have work to do" if policymakers do not gain confidence that inflation is heading down to 2%.

"The breadth of the price pressures makes the report especially difficult to dismiss. This is not simply an energy story; underlying inflation remains elevated across a wide range of categories."

— Olu Sonola, head of U.S. economics, Fitch Ratings

Impact & Analysis

What makes the August report uncomfortable is how many categories contributed. Some of the largest price increases came from technology: computer software and accessory prices rose 25.4% over the 12 months ended in August, the largest annual increase on record, while computers and smart home assistants cost 8.4% more than a year ago — fallout from surging chip costs tied to booming AI demand. Smartphone prices fell 12.2% from last year. Airfares, hotel rates, telecommunications, rental cars, vehicle maintenance, day care, nursing homes, and in-home care all posted strong gains.

The rising cost of eldercare and childcare is tied to shortages of immigrant workers, who make up a large share of the care economy, KPMG chief economist Diane Swonk noted Friday. Some 330,000 Haitians lost their Temporary Protected Status at the end of July — about 200,000 of them workers, with more than half estimated to work in the care economy.

Not everyone is convinced a hike is the right medicine. "The combination of higher energy prices and higher rates could slow the economy much more than a casual 'tap on the brakes' that a quarter-point rate hike would imply," Mike Skordeles, head of U.S. economics at Truist Advisory Services, told CNN, pointing to inconsistent job growth — employers added 162,000 jobs last month, but only a combined 52,000 in July and June.

Diaspora Angle

A rate hike lands directly on household balance sheets: higher borrowing costs for mortgages, auto loans, and credit cards, against better yields for savers. The difference between a hold and a quarter-point hike is measured in real dollars on a monthly mortgage payment — material for anyone house-hunting or refinancing this fall. A stronger dollar on the back of higher U.S. rates would also stretch remittance budgets in the other direction, making transfers to India buy fewer rupees.

What's Next

All eyes turn to the FOMC meeting Tuesday and Wednesday, where policymakers will also release updated economic projections. The August PCE report — the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, due September 30 — will capture the post-meeting data, with economists' early estimates for core PCE ranging from 3.2% to 3.3% year over year. Labor market data and the path of energy prices through the Hormuz standoff will decide whether September's move, if it comes, is a one-off or the start of a new tightening cycle.
